$comment: Role definitions for the three-book GitBook documentation template. A project may override any part by placing a file with the same shape at <docs-root>/.docs-template.json; keys given there replace the defaults role by role.

user.purpose: Entry-level getting-started book. Plain language, no jargon, for people who use the product day to day.

required_pages.why: An entry-level book without a short, timed walk-through sends newcomers straight into reference material.
The task-oriented middle of the book: what to say or do for each common job.
Readers need one page that says what they can rely on and what never leaves their machine.
The page people land on when something breaks; without it they open issues or give up.
Every book defines its own words so a reader never has to leave the book to understand it.
Concrete stories help a reader decide whether the product fits them.

operator.purpose: Low-level, detailed development and deployment guide: how the system works inside, how to install, configure, tune, monitor and operate it.

required_pages.why: The mental model every later chapter assumes; without it configuration pages are lists of knobs.
The deployment half of this book's purpose.
A complete, look-up-able reference is what distinguishes this book from the user guide.
Every command and flag the binary accepts, so nothing is only discoverable from --help.
An operator cannot run what they cannot observe.
Day-two work: backup, restore, repair, capacity, troubleshooting, release.
Technical books accumulate project-specific terms; a glossary keeps them findable.

tester.purpose: Quality-assurance guide: how every change is checked, how to run, read, explore and add tests.

required_pages.why: The first thing a tester does is run everything once; the book must make that one page.
A map from product area to test files, so a reviewer can find the tests for a change.
What blocks a merge, and why, is the contract between the team and the code.
Which kind of test to write for which kind of change, plus the pull-request checklist.
Tests miss things; the book should say how to look for them by hand.
Testing vocabulary (golden, baseline, gate, invariant) differs from the product's; define it.
